item.title: The Digital Iron Curtain
item.description: Having strangled the traditional press, the Russian state now moves to sever its own people from the open internet — throttling and listing whole platforms, dreaming of an electronic plebiscite that would abolish even the parliament. And in doing so it collides with a fact larger than itself: the global platforms have become powers in their own right, rivals of states for the human mind.

item.title: Russia Has Never Had a Free Press: Propaganda Is Not Journalism
item.description: Russia's press was never an information service; it was born as an instrument of propaganda. And propaganda, being a chemical blow to public consciousness, is not journalism at all but something closer to a controlled substance.

item.title: Shura Burtin’s Journalism on Russia’s War in Ukraine: Themes, Tone, and Bias
item.description: A comprehensive review of Shura Burtin’s body of journalistic work, focusing on recurring themes, political framing, and his portrayals of Ukraine and Russia.

item.title: Words Are Deeds: Against the Counsel to Ignore What Leaders Say
item.description: A defense of taking political rhetoric seriously: the words of the powerful are themselves a material force that moves markets, launders aggression, and reshapes what people plan and do. The fashionable advice to judge leaders only by deeds is not worldly wisdom but a disarming mistake.
